#3199. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s almost time to return to Panem as the next chapter of “The Hunger Games,” “Sunrise on the Reaping,” arrives in theaters on Friday (Nov. 20). It’ll tell the story of the 50th annual Hunger Games, known as the Quarter Quell, when a certain Haymitch Abernathy stepped into the arena. As a “Hunger Games” superfan, I can’t wait to watch it. Yes, my tickets are booked!

If you’re also feeling the hype, you might be looking for a few dystopian movies to keep you fed until “Sunrise on the Reaping." And that’s why I’ve rounded up a trio of worthwhile picks to keep you entertained until you can head to your nearest multiplex. There’s a Japanese thriller that also focuses on a teen deathmatch, a YA adaptation that is actually good (a real rarity), and a Spielberg movie that’s a pop culture-stuffed high-tech adventure.

These dystopian movies will keep your “Hunger Games” hype high until you can watch “Sunrise on the Reaping” in cinemas later this week.

You can’t discuss “The Hunger Games” franchise without somebody popping up to declare “it’s just a ‘Battle Royale’ rip-off.” While I think that argument is pretty asinine, I definitely agree that any fans of “Hunger Games” should check out this 2000 Japanese dystopian action-thriller. It also centers on a group of teens forced to fight to the death, but the Panem pageantry is stripped away. This deathmatch is even more visceral and significantly more violent — “Battle Royale” got an R-rating for very good reason.

Set in a Japan besieged by juvenile delinquency, the government institutes a yearly event called Battle Royale, in which a random high school class is taken to a remote island, each is given a duffle bag containing an assortment of supplies and a random weapon, and then they have three days to kill or be killed. Without the sci-fi trappings of “The Hunger Games,” “Battle Royale” focuses squarely on the horrors of children being forced to fight to the death.

In the wake of “The Hunger Games’” success (and “Twilight” before it), Hollywood studios scrambled to adapt any YA novel they could get their hands on. This led to awful films like “Beautiful Creatures,” “The Giver,” and “The Mortal Instruments” (to name just a few). Most didn’t even get one sequel, let alone adapt the whole series, but a rare success story was “The Maze Runner,” which actually completed its franchise run, with a full trilogy.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Based on the novels by James Dashner, “The Maze Runner” movie took the right lessons from “Hunger Games” with a solid young cast, headlined by Dylan O’Brien, and smart direction. It follows a teenage boy named Thomas (O’Brien) who awakens in a vast clearing surrounded by a gigantic stone maze. Along with his fellow teens trapped in the mysterious place, he has to solve the maze to earn his freedom and learn why he was placed there.

The sequels, “The Scorch Trials” and “The Death Cure,” are also pretty good. Though book purists will be disappointed to learn they substantially differ from the novels, stripping away the narrative twists of Dashner’s written work in favor of a more streamlined Hollywood approach.

Watch "The Maze Runner" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

Dystopian movies don’t have to be excessively dour. Case in point, Steven Spielberg’s “Ready Player One,” which is full of color, larger-than-life set pieces and endless references to decades gone by, especially the 1980s. In fact, there are probably too many pop culture references, though in fairness to Spielberg, that is also a common criticism of the Ernest Cline novel on which the movie is based. Despite its flaws — it’s a theme park movie, fun in the moment, but also artificial — “Ready Player One” is a breezy watch, and a big midpoint sequence pays homage to one of the best Kubrick flicks ever.

Set in 2045, it’s a grim time for humanity. The population escapes the bleakness of the real world via the Oasis, a virtual reality construct where people can be anything they want. When the Oasis’ creator, James Halliday (Mark Rylance), dies, a posthumous recording kickstarts a hunt through the virtual world for three Easter Eggs; whoever finds the final one will be granted control of the digital universe. Our hero is Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan), who is hoping to find the prize before a sinister corporation.

Rory is a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom’s Guide based in the UK. He covers a wide range of topics but with a particular focus on gaming and streaming. When he’s not reviewing the latest games, searching for hidden gems on Netflix, or writing hot takes on new gaming hardware, TV shows and movies, he can be found attending music festivals and getting far too emotionally invested in his favorite football team.

#3196. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

#3194. Paramount+ Orders ‘Clandestine’ Drama Series Starring Brit Marling & Tilda Swinton From ‘The OA’ Creators

EXCLUSIVE: Clandestine, a new series from The OA and A Murder At the End of the World creators Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij, is a go at Paramount+ with Marling and Tilda Swinton starring, Deadline has learned. A high-stakes family drama set in the world of D.C.’s political elite, Clandestine is produced by independent studio Sister Pictures, part of Sister Group.

The series had been developed and greenlighted by the previous Paramount+ regime under former Paramount Chair of Direct-to-Consumer Cindy Holland, I hear. The process of Swinton’s casting was well underway when the October close of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger brought along a leadership change, with Paramount+ added to the purview of HBO and HBO Max content chief Casey Bloys who became Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Direct-To-Consumer, for the combined Skydance company. Holland exited on the eve of the deal close, with her close associate, Paramount+ Head of Originals Jane Wiseman, who had steered the development on Clandestine, departing a couple of weeks later. Related Stories Casting Scott Speedman To Guest Star On 'Landman' Season 3 News 'Frisco King' Trailer: Samuel L. Jackson "Is Gonna Rob This Place Blind" In Taylor Sheridan's 'Tulsa King' Spinoff

Clandestine is now being overseen by Francesca Orsi, President, HBO Drama Series and Films, I hear. Watch on Deadline

In the new structure, Wiseman’s team reports to former HBO Max Head of Originals Aubrey, who became Head of Paramount+, Max Originals and International Programming, adding oversight of all Paramount+ programming.

As Deadline reported last month, Aubrey and HBO veteran Orsi have been reviewing Paramount+’s drama slate, with Orsi taking on projects that have a prestige drama feel similar to HBO’s brand. In addition to Clandestine, I hear Orsi also is overseeing Paramount+’s legal thriller Discretion, starring Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning, and 9/11 first responders limited series The Best of Us, headlined by Succession‘s Jeremy Strong.

There has been talk about some Paramount+ drama series potentially moving to HBO but, at least as of now, all of the streamer’s shows are staying put.

According to sources, Marling and Batmanglij started developing the project at Sister while Holland was Global CEO there. Holland left the indie studio in October 2024 to become a senior adviser to then-Skydance CEO David Ellison before becoming DTC Chair for Paramount Skydance post-merger in August 2025.

Marling and Batmanglij took out their script this past spring with Marling attached to star. Paramount+ landed Clandestine in a bidding war with FX, and HBO, I hear. Paramount+ and FX vying for Clandestine made sense as their top executives had commissioned Marling and Batmanglij’s two previous series: Paramount+’s Holland had developed and ordered The OA while running English-language scripted originals at Netflix (in addition to being involved in Clandestine early on), and FX chief John Landgraf and his team developed and picked up A Murder At the End of the World.

This also marks a full-circle moment for Orsi who is now overseeing the series she once bid on.

Clandestine is believed to have received an informal green light as part of Paramount+’s winning bid. While I hear the pickup was not cast-contingent, casting key roles was considered crucial, which explains why the streamer did not announce the series order but instead proceeded with securing the other leads opposite Marling. The process, which started over the summer, is ongoing.

Clandestine is written and executive produced by Marling, Batmanglij, Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani (Informer, The Mauritanian). Jane Featherstone (Chernobyl, Black Doves) executive produces for Sister Pictures. Blake Holland (The OA, A Murder at the End of the World) and Alice Tyler (Coldwater, The Following Events are Based on a Pack of Lies) are co-executive producers; Callum Devrell-Cameron (Lord of the Flies, Black Doves S2) a producer.

This marks the biggest TV series commitment to date for Oscar winner Swinton who starred in two British miniseries at the start of her career. Her recent feature credits include Pedro Almodóvar’s The Room Next Door, Edward Berger’s Ballad of a Small Player and Joshua Oppenheimer’s The End. She is repped by CAA, UK’s Hamilton Hodell and Peikoff Mahan Law.

Marling and Batmanglij broke out with their 2011 indie movie Sound of My Voice, which the two wrote, Batmanglij directed and Marling co-starred in. Premiering at Sundance, it earned Indie Spirit Award nominations for Best First Feature and Best Supporting Actress (Marling). They are repped by CAA and Hansen Jacobson Teller.

#3193. You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.

Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October. Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”

Powered by the new Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.

Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.

Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.

Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.

Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.

Users are reporting unexpected iCloud sign-outs on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures or unknown errors when trying to sign back in.

Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect.

The number of "coincidental" system failure happening these days make it difficult to believe it's not cyberattacks, AI failures, or both. Even more suspicious is that they all seem to be reciting the same script for the cause: "an internal update".

The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage.

Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

Are Apple services working for you? Let us know what you’re seeing in the comments.

Update: Apple now says an internal update caused the outage, ruling out a cyber attack, and many services are coming back online. Consumer-facing services are back online. Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.

Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.

#3188. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab shows a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”

The iPhone Duo comes with a few trade-offs you shouldn't have to accept on a $2,000 phone; one of which is the lack of Face ID. We know Apple's engineers are prioritising it for the inevitable iPhone Duo 2, but while we wait, an iOS 27 update could bridge the gap.

The iOS 27.3 beta introduces a new facial unlock option for iPhone Duo owners using the device's front-facing camera. It's a bit like Face ID Lite: users will need to authenticate with Touch ID every 45 minutes to use it, and they'll still need to resort to Touch ID for certain actions, like authorizing Apple Pay or filling in logins from Passwords.

Duo users will only be able to use the Unlock with Front Camera feature on the external 5.4-inch display. So, if the phone is unfolded, you can't use the under-display camera on the inner screen to achieve the same result.

Unlock with Front Camera can be found in the Touch ID & Passcode menu in your settings. However, you'll need to have an Apple Developer account and be running the iOS 27.3 developer beta before you can enable it.

If you want to try it for yourself, remember to be careful when installing beta software and ideally create a backup of your iPhone first. Once you're running the beta, switching the feature on is a simple toggle.

Go to your Settings app and scroll down to TouchID & Passcode. Tap the option and enter your passcode to proceed.

You'll see the option to toggle on Unlock with Front Camera. Tap it.

Similar to when you set up Face ID, you'll need to let the iPhone Duo scan your face to activate the feature. Once you've rotated your face, and looked at the camera, you're good to go.

As a leftie, I've been bugged by the fact that I can't use Face ID on the Duo over the last couple of weeks. This new feature could alleviate a huge amount of that frustration.

After trying it myself, it's worked well but I won't go into details at this stage, because it's still early days. Unlock with Front Camera hasn't yet made it to the iOS 27.3 public beta.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

That being said, for those times when you're juggling the Duo one-handed, I can see this addition being a huge bonus. There will, of course, be some limitations, since the Duo's front camera isn't a full TrueDepth camera system. That means you won't be able to unlock it in full darkness and it's less secure — potentially leaving it open to being spoofed by a similar-looking face.

I can also forsee the 45-minute timeout tripping folks up a time or two, though. For most of my workday, the Duo rests either face up or in Tent Mode, and it's easy for 45 minutes to go by without checking — especially if you have one of the best Apple Watches serving you notifications.

We'll dig into how this works over the long term when it becomes a fully public feature but, in the meantime, if there are other potential Duo features you'd like to see added to iOS, let me know about them in the comments.

#3185. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3184. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

#3183. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Making a cafe-quality coffee at home requires at least two of these three things: a great machine, high-quality coffee beans, and someone who knows what they're doing. A well-trained barista can make pro-level coffee on a mid-level machine, as long as they use great beans. An untrained barista will get a top-notch brew with a premium machine and high-quality beans. A trained barista doesn't require expensive beans to make a perfect coffee, as long as they have a good machine.

See what I mean? So what happens if you have a fancy espresso machine and no barista experience? You need to learn how to use it — which a lot of us simply don't have time for. Why learn how to make good coffee at home when you can get fantastic coffee at the cafe down the street?

Don't fret, though. I just got an exclusive first look at Breville's (Sage) brand-new espresso machine, the Barista Express Neo, and I think it's about to change the coffee game due to one unprecedented, patented feature.

Although only available in the U.K. upon initial release, the Breville/Sage Barista Express Neo is one of the coffee scene's most exciting new arrivals. With the patented SmoothSip technology, say goodbye to dialing in and wasting espresso shots.

Breville/Sage have slapped a very Breville/Sage-coded name onto this feature: SmoothSip(TM). It's in the same vein as Ninja's "NeverClog" blender: a little wacky, although overwhelmingly "We're a corporation, but we're relatable, right, kids?"

SageSpeak nomenclature aside, SmoothSip is genuinely innovative. In short, it's a game changer.

So what does SmoothSip actually do? During extraction, SmoothSip live-adjusts bar pressure to ensure every espresso shot pulls — regardless of a too-fine or too-coarse grind size. How many shots have you wasted due to an incorrect grind size? Mine's definitely in the hundreds.

In theory, if you grind your coffee on step 20 — Breville's default — it will be too coarse, unless you're using really oily, dark beans. But with SmoothSip, the machine will slow down the pump (and, yes, lower that pressure below 9 bars) to extract a 1:2 ratio espresso within 26 seconds.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Think of it like a car engine. If you need to drive 1 mile in 2 minutes, you should drive at 30MPH, right? That will necessitate a steady press on the gas pedal. But what if your car is going at 40MPH? You'll need to apply the brake to slow back down to 30.

That's exactly what SmoothSip is doing — it's slowing down the machine (or speeding it up, if your grind is too fine) to reach that destination in the allotted time.

In short: yes. Yes, espresso is "supposed" to extract at 9 bars of pressure. Obviously, reducing the pressure from 9 bars to 3 bars or up to 15 bars isn't ideal in the grand scheme of coffee nerdiness.

However, after each assisted shot, the machine tells you which grind size you should adjust to. And, at the end of the day, you still get your espresso. Even though it's not "perfect", I would rather drink a slightly "imperfect" espresso shot over a nonexistent espresso shot.

I made an overextracted espresso shot on the original Breville Barista Express and the new Barista Express Neo. While they were both too sour, the Neo shot had a much richer mouthfeel and a better depth of flavor. It was tangibly more drinkable than the Barista Express shot.

The Barista Express Neo isn't just a one-trick pony — even though the SmoothSip trick is pretty neat.

The Neo also has an Acaia scale built in, so it always grinds between 17.6-18g of coffee. Yes, Acaia, as in Pearl S and Lunar fame — but this time you're not paying $200+ for the privilege of weighing out your coffee.

There's also a Baratza grinder built in, which cost between $199 (Baratza Encore ESP) and $899 (Baratza Forte BG). If we go off previous Breville models, the Neo will have a version of the $200 Encore ESP grinder.

As with all Breville machines, the Neo has a PID controller to adjust water temperature throughout the brewing process.

Of course, there's a powerful steam wand — but I noticed it took a while to heat up. Perhaps this was just a demo-sample issue. I'll get to the bottom of it when I review the Barista Express Neo myself.

As you might be able to discern from the £ sign above, the Breville/Sage Barista Express Neo is only available in the U.K. right now. It will come to the U.S., but there's no set calendar date. I believe it will be some time later in 2026, but without a concrete date, I'm reticent to speculate.

Unfortunately, across-the-pond-ers will need to wait for the Neo to make it to their esteemed continent. I'm not sure when that will be, but in the meantime, I'm going to be drinking enough Neo coffee to give me the shakes.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

#3177. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3176. These Noise-Canceling Skullcandy Headphones Are 50% Off Ahead of Black Friday

Black Friday is an excellent time to score a new pair of headphones that would otherwise be a splurge, with retailers like Amazon and Walmart already offering massive discounts on tech essentials from top brands a week ahead of the holiday. One of the early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar is the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones, a mid-range noise-canceling option that’s perfect for bass lovers and is currently 50% off, dropping to $119.99 (originally $239.99).

PCMag says they deliver “brain-rattling levels of bass” and have a comfortable fit, with generous memory foam cushioning and minimal clamping pressure that lends itself well to long listening sessions. The aesthetic is nothing to scoff at either, with a refined and modern style. It’s worth noting they also come in a hardshell zip-up case with a fabric-lined exterior.

Powered by 40mm dynamic drivers, they offer reliable noise cancellation with the ANC slider set to max on the companion app, which lets users adjust a range of controls and listening modes, including the intensity of bass. The bass boost feature is ideal for those seeking bass-heavy headphones, but may be overwhelming for those who prefer a more balanced sound.

Battery life lasts around 50 to 60 hours per charge, with Skullcandy claiming that you get four hours of listening time from around 10 minutes of charging. While brands like Bose will outperform in ANC quality, if you’re looking for noise-canceling audio gear that checks most boxes at a reasonable price point, the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are a smart choice, especially at over $100 off.

#3175. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

Read more: iOS 27 revamps AirPods settings in a big way, here’s the new design

Which AirPods features in iOS 27 are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

If you’re counting down the minutes until you can play the game for yourself, I’m bringing you live updates on GTA 6 reviews and beyond. Plus, I’ve also found a selection of GTA 6 Black Friday deals if you want to upgrade your setup before playing for yourself.

Granted, my life is different now, so I won't be able to completely sink every waking hour into GTA 6, but that means I can better appreciate the time I will have with what should be another stellar entry.

Only the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes close to matching this level of critical praise. It'll be interesting to see what audiences have to say once the game is available.

Okay, so GTA 6 isn't launching on PC (I'm sure a PC port is coming in 2027), but the fine folks over at PC Gamer got their hands on an early copy and put together a report after 100 hours of gameplay. Writer Christopher Livingston was very impressed with the game but did note, "it will be (mostly) so much greater when it comes to PC." Maybe when GTA 6 arrives on PC, we'll get the 60 fps mode of our dreams!

Dave LeClair, Managing Editor, checking in. I was going to wait a bit for GTA VI, since the little time I get to play video games now is pretty much locked down by Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

However, after seeing these review scores, I might have a hard time waiting to get the biggest video game release of all time. I might have to jump on my Xbox Series X and plunk down the cash for a pre-order so I can get some time in this weekend.

So I turn to you, our readers, with a poll:

Midnight already felt so far away, but these reviews are making the wait feel extra long. Of course, some parts of the world are already playing GTA 6 right now! If you didn't know, Rockstar hasn't gone for a single global unlock time; instead, GTA 6 will be playable at midnight local time in your region. You can check how long you have left to wait via this nifty fan-made GTA 6 countdown clock. I've got 10 hours to go!

There was some controversy yesterday when GTA 6 was nominated for eight Game Awards, including GOTY, without it being available to the public. Those nominations certainly don't look undeserved now, based on the reviews that have just dropped. At this point, you would have to say that GTA 6 looks like the clear favorite to win GOTY.

More reviews have gone live, and as of writing, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game on Metacritic. It's at an astonishing 99 after 146 reviews. While the original Ocarina of Time also boasts a 99 score, that's from a much smaller sample size of just 22 reviews (it's a game from 1998, before the explosion in online game reviews). This score could change as more reviews are published, and post-launch reviews could be more critical, but so far, it's holding. GTA 6 really is getting unprecedented review scores.

If you had any doubts about pre-ordering GTA 6, these reviews might have swayed you. The game is getting perfect scores across the board, and is being described as "the game of the generation." You can still lock-in your pre-order, and if you opt for the "code in box" edition you get a free poster as well (and £5 discount in the U.K.).

Another five star review comes from Gamesradar. Reviewer Josh West writes, "GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. There's a degree of sophistication to everything GTA 6 does, and there's no aspect of the series' gameplay that hasn't been improved over past instalments."

Our friends over at TechRadar, have plenty of positive things to say about GTA 6. In a 5-star review, TR's Rob Dwiar, says, "Grand Theft Auto 6 is an absolute triumph, and one of the most complete, most gripping, and downright coolest video games I have ever played, and is an essential must-play experience."

Another GTA 6 review, another perfect score. This time from Destructoid. Their reviewer, Scott Duwe, writes, "Grand Theft Auto 6 is part criminal come-up tale, part love story, and part life sim all wrapped up in an impossibly deep and detailed Rockstar Games open world that may never run out of things to do. For the last three-plus weeks, I have been gleefully vacationing in Vice City: robbing banks, fighting drug dealers, stealing cars, and enjoying the view while not coming close to finishing everything it has to offer. GTA 6 is finally here now, and it was well worth the wait."

Wow. As of writing, Grand Theft Auto VI holds a near-perfect 99 score on Metacritic. This would tie it with the best reviewed game of all time, the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Of course, this score could fluctuate as more review scores pour in, but the game is off to one heck of a start. Could this be the best reviewed GTA in history?

"Unprecedented. Unbelievable. Unmissable." That's the strapline for IGN's GTA 6 review. Quite a way to open any review.

IGN's reviewer, Luke Reilly, says, "GTA 6 has not stopped astonishing me since I started it. I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played."

Over on review site OpenCritic, GTA 6 is off to a flying start; it's currently got a 99 average score, with 100% of critics recommending it. Rockstar looks to have delivered and then some!

VGC's Jordan Middler says, "Grand Theft Auto 6 is a modern masterpiece. Rockstar's developers have created a remarkable open world that excels in storytelling, gameplay, visuals, music and technology to achieve something truly unmatched. Minor performance issues don’t dull the sparkle of an absolute must-play experience. GTA 6 was more than worth the wait." VGC has given GTA 6 a full 5/5!

GTA 6 reviews are going live, and the first one I've spotted is from Giant Bomb, their reviewer, Dan Ryckert, has given the game a full 5 stars, and said:

"Grand Theft Auto VI is Rockstar’s best game. In terms of inspiring awe at how far video games have come, I can only compare it to formative experiences of mine like playing Super Mario 64 or Metal Gear Solid for the first time. In the thirteen years between entries of one of the biggest franchises in entertainment, fans’ expectations grew to a level that felt unrealistic. Somehow, Rockstar has managed to overdeliver on the most hyped video game of all time."

After 13 years of waiting, it's a little surreal to say that GTA 6 arrives in just 10 minutes. If you live in New Zealand. Rockstar has opted for a staggered release time, with the game "unlocking" at midnight in your specific region. Because of timezones, this means the lucky folks in New Zealand can enter Vice City first (I'm not jealous...).

Reminder, it's also been reported that GTA 6 reviews will drop as the game goes live in New Zealand, so we might be minutes away from getting our first critical impressions of GTA 6 as well. Should (hopefully) be lots to discuss very soon.

A big decision when it comes to GTA 6 is which version to get, the standard or the Ultimate Edition, which costs an extra $20, but comes with plenty of extra digital goodies. Let me know which edition of the game you've gone for in the poll above.

If you're planning to play GTA 6 on PS5, there's an important update that you need to download first. Yesterday, PlayStation released a new PS5 system software update (version 26.07-14.23.00), and over on X, PlayStation Support US confirmed you will need to download it on your console before playing GTA 6 tomorrow. The post reads:

"Sony Interactive has issued a PS5 system software update that is required before playing Grand Theft Auto VI. Players should download this update prior to midnight on November 19 so that they’re ready to play on launch day, November 19."

So, even if you're already pre-loaded GTA 6, make sure to switch on your PS5 and get the update downloaded to your console ahead of the game unlocking at midnight.

I've seen a lot of online debate about GTA 6's Metacritic score. As of writing, the highest scored game of 2026 is the Ocarina of Time remake at 96. Meanwhile, GTA 5 scored an impressive 97 back in 2013, and GTA 4 got a stunning 98. Where do you think GTA 6 will land on the popular review aggregate site. Let me know in the poll.

GTA 6 reviews aren't even live yet, and already the game has been nominated for a slew of awards at the upcoming Game Awards 2026. It's up for eight awards, including Game of the Year. Other nominees for the event's top honor include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, 007: First Light, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem and Control Resonant. That's great company to be in, and it would suggest that GTA 6 won't disappoint! You can check out the full list of nominees here.

Of course, the single biggest question today is when exactly GTA 6 reviews will appear. Rockstar hasn't officially confirmed when critics will start delivering their verdicts on the game. However, a recent article from Insider Gaming claims that GTA 6 reviews are embargoed until today (November 18) at 3 a.m. PT / 6 a.m. ET / 11 a.m. GMT. That would mean GTA 6 reviews in less than an hour. But without word from Rockstar, this reporting should be taken with a grain of salt. It's not confirmed.

Good morning! It's going to be a big day for anybody excited for GTA 6. Reviews are expected to drop, and the game will start going live (the lucky folks in New Zealand are up first). There's plenty to talk about, so let's dive into the latest GTA 6 updates.

#3173. iOS 27.3’s redesigned Apple Health app requires newer iPhone model

iOS 27.3 will introduce an all-new Apple Health experience when it ships next month, but you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get it. Here’s why.

When iOS 27.3 launches next month, it will include a variety of upgrades for Apple TV, Apple Music, Siri AI, iCloud+, the iPhone Duo, and more.

Another tentpole addition is an all-new Apple Health app, which was first unveiled back in September when new Apple Watch models debuted.

The Health app is getting a full revamp in iOS 27.3 that’s meant to be more personalized and informative than ever. New features include an Insights tab, Longevity tab, educational videos, at-home movement evaluations, and more.

But for many iPhone users who update to iOS 27.3, the Health app might remain largely unchanged. Why? Because the new experience relies on Apple Intelligence, so you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get it.

That means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer is required.

If you have an older iPhone model, or simply have chosen not to enable Apple Intelligence on your device, you’ll miss out on the new Health features. They’ll also only be available in select languages initially.

These forthcoming Health upgrades join the 20+ other new Apple Intelligence features that recently debuted in iOS 27.

Have you tried the new Health app in iOS 27.3? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.
