#3134. Bullish (BLSH) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Crypto headwinds weighed, but the pending Equiniti deal reshapes the outlook.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 3:55PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Bullish (BLSH +5.66%) reported third quarter results that included 10% adjusted revenue growth and a 42% adjusted EBITDA margin despite what management characterized as a deep crypto bear market. The company is preparing for the closing of the Equiniti acquisition in Jan. 2027, which will expand its service base to approximately 3,000 public companies and 20 million shareholders. Management stated that the combined entity expects to realize up to $100 million in cost reductions over the medium term and generate more than $1 billion in cumulative free cash flow. Strategic focus remains on tokenizing actual issuer shares through a newly formed coalition and expanding into the U.S. derivatives market.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Bullish Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Liam Foley, Director of Corporate Development. Please go ahead.

Liam Foley: Good morning, and welcome to our third quarter earnings call. I'm Liam Foley, Director of Corporate Development, and I'm joined on today's call by our Chief Executive Officer, Tom Farley, and Chief Financial Officer, David Bonanno. This call will contain forward-looking statements, including those relating to our expected performance and business opportunities, our pending acquisition of Equiniti Group, the anticipated benefits and strategic rationale of the transaction, expected timing and closing conditions, the combined company's targets and business opportunities following the transaction, our tokenization of securities and the adoption of tokenized securities, and our share repurchase program. These statements are not assurances of future performance and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially.

Such risks include, among others, the possibility that the Equiniti transaction may not be completed, failure to obtain required regulatory approvals, the possibility that anticipated benefits may not be realized and risks related to the integration of Equiniti's business, the evolving legal and regulatory environment for digital assets and tokenized securities, and the timing and extent of any share repurchases. For more details on these and other risks, please refer to today's earnings press release and our SEC filings, including our 20-F dated March 9, 2026. We undertake no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements. This call will also include a discussion of non-IFRS financial measures.

A reconciliation to the most directly comparable IFRS metrics can be found in our earnings press release and presentation, which also contain additional information regarding non-IFRS financial measures and key performance indicators. I'll now turn the call over to Tom.

Thomas Farley: Thank you, Liam. Very thorough. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining. This morning, Bullish reported strong third quarter results despite significant macro headwinds and the full throes of the crypto bear market. We grew adjusted revenue 10% year-over-year, subscription, services, and other revenue 13% year-over-year, and we expanded our adjusted EBITDA margin to 42%. Our growth is testament to our success building a business that can perform across cycles. Looking forward, I want to discuss 4 things: a key leadership addition, Equiniti, tokenization and capital allocation. Then Dave will take you through the figures. First, leadership.

Last week, we announced that Stacey Cunningham, my former colleague and the former President of the New York Stock Exchange, has joined Bullish as President. She was my Chief Operating Officer at the New York Stock Exchange, and she succeeded me as President when she became the first woman to lead the exchange in 220 years. Stacey and I worked closely at the New York Stock Exchange to build a new, efficient and performant exchange and post-trade technology environment that was both value-added for customers and far less expensive to provide. The result was a business that grew earnings dramatically over many years.

Stacey's relationships and experience working with thousands of issuers will be invaluable as we pull together all the pieces of modern market infrastructure focused on the needs of those issuers. We believe that when 1 of the most respected leaders in capital markets chooses to build the next generation of market infrastructure at Bullish, it tells you where this company and this industry are headed. Second, Equiniti. We remain on track to close in early January 2027. Antitrust clearances are behind us. And in October, we received a series of change of control approvals. What remains are a couple of final regulatory approvals before we are all systems go.

The terms are the same as the ones we announced in May, the assumption of about $1.85 billion of debt and the exchange of roughly 60 million Bullish shares based on the $38.48 share price set when we signed. We've used these 6 months to be ready on day 1. Day 1 plans are set and the technology roadmap is clear. One modern platform for transfer agency and share plans, one portal for issuers, shareholders and employees alike and tokenization built directly into the register itself. We aim to deliver issuers and shareholders with an upgraded and enhanced experience from day 1, capable of handling all their share-related needs, whether it be paper, electronic or tokenized shares. Shifting to tokenization.

We've seen a technology transition like this before. Shares first moved from paper certificates to electronic records, and now they are moving on-chain. The importance and nature of an issuer's actual share itself doesn't change, but the rails underlying it do. We believe the move from electronic to tokenized is just as inevitable as the move from paper to electronic and for the same reasons: it is faster, more efficient and far cheaper. The economics are too powerful to ignore. For banks, brokers and market infrastructure providers, we believe that the immediate and transparent nature of on-chain shares can unlock many hundreds of billions of dollars of trapped collateral and take billions of cost out of the system.

For issuers, it is a technology upgrade that brings them new benefits. Over the past few months, we have met with a significant portion of Equiniti's roughly 3,000 issuers to discuss this technology upgrade. We walk them through how issuer tokenization differs from other forms and help them prepare for this upgrade. At launch, issuer tokens solve real problems: always-on markets that settle in seconds, a real-time view of cap table non-objecting beneficial owners, and access to investors across more venues, geographies and hours.

Looking ahead beyond launch, we expect issuers to build on this infrastructure in ways that open up new use cases and new growth, including a deeper connection with their shareholders, such as by the provision of discounts, loyalty points or other perks that are provided directly to investors' on-chain wallets as a reward for loyal shareholding. With Bullish's relationships in crypto and Equiniti's roughly 3,000 public company issuers, we believe we are at the center of this effort to bring equities into the digital age and to build this next generation of infrastructure. In September, we launched the Issuer Token Coalition with Equiniti.

Members include many brokers such as Alpaca, Apex, DriveWealth and SoFi; market makers such as QRT, DRW and Flow Traders; infrastructure providers such as Superstate, Vertalo and Zero Hash; and exchanges, including the New York Stock Exchange. This coalition is working through the standards and mechanics for the actual shares of listed companies to reside on public blockchains. This will catalyze the evolution from paper to electronic and to now our on-chain future. You may have read news about issuers rejecting so-called tokenized shares. These stories were referring to third-party tokens, where the tokens in question are definitively not the issuer's actual shares and are rather some form of IOU entitlement or other type of derivative.

That is not what either the Issuer Token Coalition or Bullish is working on. We are working with the issuers on their actual shares, and these conversations are well received. The demand for issuer tokens is real and growing, and we will share more of our exciting plans post closing of our Equiniti transaction. As mentioned on prior earnings calls, the largest unknown for me is the pace of adoption of tokenization technology and when exactly growth will meaningfully accelerate. However, we feel better now than ever about the tokenization opportunity and the probability of that being a long-term growth driver for us. Our existing businesses tallied solid results during a soft market in this quarter.

We added institutional flow globally and onboarded or are in the process of onboarding various clients, including SoFi, StoneX and others. Marex, with more than 3,400 institutional clients, now sources liquidity from Bullish. Our derivatives licensing efforts in the United States are moving forward, and we continue to expect access -- pardon me, we continue to expect to access the U.S. derivatives market far sooner than we had originally believed. Liquidity Services remained resilient in the quarter despite lighter crypto activity and prices. CoinDesk Indices continued to win new product mandates and CoinDesk Media maintained its position as the leading crypto news business. Finally, turning to capital allocation. Our Board authorized a share repurchase program of up to $300 million.

We believe our shares are undervalued at current prices, and we have conviction in our long-term trajectory. Dave will walk you through the details.

David Bonanno: Thanks, Tom, and good morning, everyone. This morning, we filed our third quarter results and shareholder update Form 6-K, including reconciliations of our non-IFRS measures discussed on the call. Turning to our third quarter results on Page 10. Total adjusted revenue was $84.4 million, up 10% year-over-year, with subscription, services, and other revenue of $56.3 million, up 13% year-over-year, and adjusted transaction revenue of $28 million, up 5% year-over-year. Third quarter adjusted operating expenses were $48.7 million, resulting in adjusted EBITDA of $35.6 million at a 42% margin. Finally, adjusted net income was $18.7 million, up 35% year-over-year. Turning to Bullish's full year guidance on Page 18.

We are narrowing our previously provided range for SS&O revenue to $225 million to $235 million and lowering our previously provided range for adjusted operating expenses to $220 million to $225 million. These updates reflect both the challenging crypto environment, including lower prices and the failure to pass the Clarity Act, as well as our response to those conditions, including execution of meaningful efficiencies actioned during the third quarter. Finally, we raised and narrowed our full year 2026 finance expense outlook to $60 million to $65 million to account for a higher interest rate environment and outlook for the remainder of the year.

As a reminder, we do not guide on adjusted transaction revenue, and our monthly trading metrics are available on our IR website. Next, I'll turn to Equiniti's full year 2026 outlook as shown on Page 20. We now expect total revenue of $910 million to $965 million, including $220 million to $240 million of interest income, and adjusted EBITDA less CapEx of $360 million to $370 million. This outlook is essentially unchanged from the one we provided in May with the exception of approximately $20 million in revenue coming from a large event, which we have broken out separately. Equiniti will occasionally generate outsized revenue from uniquely large or prolonged corporate actions such as extended proxy campaigns or M&A activity.

While these large events do occasionally occur, they are infrequent and unpredictable. And as such, we do not forecast them and encourage investors to exclude them from the normalized revenue base of the company. Turning to our combined medium-term outlook on Page 21. We continue to expect revenue growth to ramp up throughout the period, albeit at a slower pace over the near term, which reflects some of the headwinds I previously mentioned. For operating expenses and profitability, we now expect net cost reductions of $75 million to $100 million over the medium-term outlook as compared to the combined 2026 cost base, up from our prior guidance of $25 million to $50 million in net cost reductions.

We expect the net cost savings to be front-loaded over the medium-term outlook with all actions completed by year-end 2028 and a substantial portion of total net cost reductions realized during 2027. Putting these updates together, we continue to see combined adjusted EBITDA less CapEx margins in excess of 50% by the end of the medium-term outlook as well as approximately $300 million of EBITDA less CapEx growth and more than $1 billion of cumulative free cash flow over the period. Regarding combined interest expense, D&A and other, we now forecast that line item to be between $205 million and $225 million in 2027, driven by the increasing interest rate environment.

As a reminder, these comparisons are versus Equiniti's normalized revenue and profitability, excluding large event income previously discussed. Lastly, regarding the share repurchase authorization approved by our Board, we have the financial capacity to simultaneously invest for growth, aggressively execute on the Equiniti integration and tactically create shareholder value via share repurchases when appropriate, all without compromising our ability to execute on future M&A or deleverage our balance sheet. Before handing it back to Tom, I want to provide some additional important disclosures on the share repurchase authorization.

Before commencing any share repurchase activities, Bullish intends to file a comprehensive financial package under Form 6-K with the SEC the week of November 30, which will include pro forma financials, Equiniti's 2024 and 2025 audited financial statements, and unaudited interim financials through September 30, 2026. As a reminder, please also refer to the additional disclosures contained in our press release and Form 6-K. With that, I'll turn it back to Tom for closing remarks.

Thomas Farley: Thank you, Dave. We came to the public markets as a crypto exchange just over a year ago. Our stated objective was to provide mission-critical products and services designed to help institutions grow their businesses, empower individual customers and drive the adoption of stablecoins, digital assets and blockchain technology. Following the expected closing of the Equiniti transaction in January, we will serve roughly 3,000 public companies and more than 20 million shareholders with the technology to bring their shares on-chain whenever they choose. Thank you. Operator, we're ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question will come from Brian Bedell from Deutsche Bank.

Brian Bedell: Congrats on Stacey joining. That's very exciting. Maybe just to start with the tokenization trajectory and plans. So, I think I heard you, Tom, clearly that you're definitely pursuing the issuer-led route as opposed to entitlement tokens. Can you talk also about, I guess, two things: One, what you view as the pace of acceptance of tokenization of issuers of tokenizing your stock? And then secondly, around trading that, to what extent do you intend to use the Tokenized Securities Venue that the SEC included within its innovation exemption or rather an ATS license?

Thomas Farley: Sure. Great questions, Brian. The Eskimo language has 10 words for snow. In crypto, we're the opposite. We have 1 word, tokenization, and it defines 10 different things. So, to be clear, you referenced the third-party tokenization. And I just want to be candid, you've read some articles about how issuers have not loved the idea of somebody else going out and tokenizing that issuer's shares and marketing them as the actual shares, and that hasn't been terribly well received. And I understand why. I'm empathetic. It introduces, in many cases, one or multiple brokers.

It introduces credit risk and operational risk and settlement risk and the issuer saying, "Wait a minute, I didn't have any control over that." That is not at all what we are doing, Brian. So, when you said, I understand you're going the issuer token route, that's the only route we've ever been going down because ultimately, we believe that the issuer tokens are going to underpin trading, settlement, clearing, ledgering of these shares, other use cases such as lending, borrowing, pledging collateral, and ultimately are going to give the issuer the ability to reward loyal shareholders along the lines I mentioned in my prepared remarks. And when we're speaking to issuers, this concept is not confronting to them.

They're comfortable as long as the thing we're talking about is their actual share that they have control over and it has all of the rights and obligations -- a shareholder benefits from all the rights and obligations of owning the actual physical share. So, I hope that answered the first part of your question. And then with respect to the second part of your question, the TSVs do allow for both third-party tokens as well as issuer tokens. But so far, what you've been reading about publicly is all about these third-party tokens.

We are working quietly in the background to make sure that issuer tokens, if these TSVs become liquid, become an actual successful venue, that these issuer tokens are plumbed in, in the appropriate way. But stay tuned for more details in that regard.

Brian Bedell: That's great color. And then a question for Dave, just on the cost save improvement from the pending Equiniti acquisition. And to what extent was that driven by the ability to use AI in a lot of their back office or back-end services? And if that wasn't part of it, what do you see as potential upside from automating a lot of their back-end processes?

David Bonanno: Thanks, Brian. I'd say the change in the increase in our expected net cost reductions over the medium-term outlook absolutely partially driven by advancements in technology such as AI and automation and then also simply us having had a lot more time to get to know the business, the people, the operations and to firm out a plan that will be executable starting on day 1. And so it's a combination of those two things. We think the advancements of technology are going to bring efficiencies to the cost base of both companies.

You've seen Bullish's ability to do that with our own cost base, taking very quick action during the third quarter in response to the macro environment, getting our own operational costs under control and back down toward the low end of the original range from back in February after we had begun experiencing some cost increases during the middle of the year. So, we are hopeful that we'll continue to experience and be able to achieve efficiencies on both cost bases going forward.

Thomas Farley: And I just wanted to add 1 note on that, Brian. This is just 1 of the many reasons I'm excited about Stacey coming aboard. At the New York Stock Exchange, when I arrived there, they had 6 different matching engine technologies that were live in some form or function. And so turning those all into a single matching engine that really delighted customers and became the envy of that marketplace was a very difficult task with no AI, no LLMs, but something that Stacey took on and achieved very impressively. We have a similar task ahead of us.

The difference is with respect to the Equiniti systems infrastructure, today, we have AI and LLMs, which enables us to do things much, much more quickly, and we're already seeing that as part of our integration efforts.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question will come from Pete Christiansen from Citi.

Peter Christiansen: Tom, I was just wondering if we can go back in time, it's been roughly a year since the IPO. And yes, the crypto markets have been kind of volatile over the last year. I'm just curious if you could share how the U.S. business has performed since receiving the BitLicense. Can you provide any metrics around like client growth, institutional adoption or trading activity, something along that lines. Just curious how that business has flourished since acquiring the BitLicense.

Thomas Farley: Yes, I appreciate it, Pete. Boy, I have a lot of great things to say, but I don't want to look like Baghdad Bob, to quote a 20-year-old reference. Crypto has been a bit of a -- you said it politely. It's been a bit of a disaster, really. I mean from the moment we IPO-ed, Bitcoin, obviously the most prominent asset, is down by half. And ultimately, we didn't get the Clarity Act across the line.

And I said on several earnings calls, while I didn't think the Clarity Act was make or break, the truth was it would give institutions a bit more comfort, a bit of a safe harbor, and we would see those institutions kind of jump in with both feet. I've met several banks in the last week or two. And it's actually been very encouraging to hear that they haven't put their plans on hold post Clarity Act. But I will note, if you look at the major U.S. banks, with one notable exception, they're still not even holding Bitcoin on behalf of their clients. So, the truth is we brought on a lot of U.S. clients.

We've made a dent in U.S. market share in a very short period of time. As I said in my prepared remarks, we're hopeful that we'll be live with our derivatives franchise here in the U.S. in the next several months, maybe even sooner, although ultimately, it's up to the regulator to decide when is the appropriate time. We've signed up, as a reminder, Morgan Stanley for their ETF franchise, which has done very, very well, launching crypto ETFs, and we are the index provider and many other anecdotes.

But the overarching macro headwinds have been so significant that the growth has been more muted than I would have expected when you and I met, Pete, back in August around the time of our IPO.

Operator: And our next question will come from Ken Worthington from JPMorgan.

Kenneth Worthington: We've seen a number of tokenization initiatives launched, including at the DTCC. Does Bullish have a role if companies tokenize at other venues? And if so, what is that role? And if DTCC launched with 34 securities, has DTCC locked up the tokenization opportunity for those companies? Or could there still be a role for Bullish with these companies in the future?

Thomas Farley: Yes, I appreciate it, Ken. There's a few questions nested in there that I'm going to do my best to unpick and not go on a long monologue. First thing I will say is we're making a lot of progress on tokenization on the Bullish side. We've announced publicly several network partners. We already have some trading venue partners as well as other trading venue partners in the works. In the fourth quarter, we have started to record revenue from multiple customers for tokenization of, in particular, equities.

And so all of that is moving forward in a positive direction, maybe even a very positive direction, but I don't want to put too big of a sheen on it, Ken, until we see it all come together post closing. With respect to the issuer side, I don't want to speak for Equiniti. We expect that transaction to close in January, at which point we will be able to provide more details about progress, specifically with respect to issuers and plans with respect to issuers.

But the net of it, Ken, is -- and I know you know this because you're as good at channel checks as anyone, the net of it is that really the whole market is coming around to the realization that the underpinning for tokenization of equities, in particular, is going to be issuer tokens in some form or fashion. And that isn't to speak ill of what you mentioned DTC or what others are doing. These third-party tokens have a role just like ADRs have a role, just like ETFs have a role.

But most important, Ken, is the actual share, and no one is doing that today because only a transfer agent working with an issuer can do that today. And it's not something to be rushed. So, no, absolutely not. I applaud DTC for making progress with their own blockchain technology. But just like DTC holds paper shares, just like DTC holds electronic shares, someday they'll hold the issuer shares as well. And so what we are building, our model fits very nicely with the advancements that you're hearing about and reading about.

Operator: Our next question will come from Owen Lau from Clear Street.

Owen Lau: First of all, congrats on the hiring of Stacey. Sticking with the tokenization theme, I know we have talked a lot already, but I saw your press release about the Issuer Token Coalition. You also had the tokenization showcase last month. I'm just curious to hear from you, Tom, under what conditions issuers are happy to tokenize their shares. Is the control over their shares their main concern? I guess more importantly, what does it take for them to tokenize their shares?

Thomas Farley: Yes. No, thank you, Owen. Really great question. And let me do this a little bit by analogy. So, Equiniti has been around for 97 years. And actually, the reason transfer agents came about is disreputable people would double sell the same share before transfer agents. And so transfer agents came about to keep track of every single share and who the holder was. And in those days, as you would imagine, those were paper shares. And so for about half a century, transfer agents kept track of who owned a paper share. And then the electronic share was introduced.

And the transfer agent added -- it didn't replace, it added the ability to keep track of electronic shares alongside the ability to keep track of paper shares. And believe it or not, in the year 2026, there is still a goodly number of paper shares in circulation and transfer agents like Equiniti and others keep track of Owen Lau owns 3 paper shares and Dave Bonanno owns 6 electronic shares, and that equals 9 total shares for this company.

What's now coming, and in fact, it has already come in the case of Bullish and others, but what will come for the 3,000 issuers is simply a technology upgrade that will enable transfer agents to keep track of shares in paper form, in electronic form and in on-chain form. But what they are keeping track of is the share itself, not a derivative, not an IOU, not an entitlement. Those latter bucket are the third-party tokens that you're reading more about, they're making more news in the press, but the far more important innovation is simply the ability to have shares on-chain.

Because that will be the bedrock, and that will enable all the use cases for issuers and for brokers to take hundreds of billions of dollars of collateral out of the system. Finally, you asked what does it take to tokenize. And Owen, that's where we work with the issuers and you write a smart contract, which is really just a piece of software. It sounds complicated. You create the shares. If somebody wants to move the shares from one public blockchain to the other, that's super simple. You just burn it on one and you mint it on the other.

And now you have a token, and you just need the ability to create it via smart contract to have a whitelist to make sure that people who are KYC/AML can hold that token. And you need the ability to keep track of it on a ledger such as operated by a transfer agent. And behind the scenes, getting all that plumbing working is what we're doing. And look, we've given you -- we've kind of sprinkled some tea leaves. I think that's a metaphor, I might be butchering it.

When we -- back in May, when we did the Equiniti transaction, the point of this transaction was to be able to provide this on-chain tracking and on-chain registry for shares for 3,000 issuers, not for 1 or 2 or 3 over here or 5 over here. So, what we're working on quietly, Owen, is a solution that can apply and can be a technology upgrade at the option of the issuers for all of the Equiniti public companies.

Operator: And our next question will come from Ed Engel from Compass Point.

Edward Engel: In the presentation, you flagged a slower ramp in tokenization and blockchain services in 2027. Does that reflect slower performance from the legacy business just amid the crypto winter? Or does that reflect maybe some slower uptake in tokenization from Equiniti customers?

David Bonanno: Thanks, Ed. That outlook does reflect the macro crypto environment we're in, some headwinds facing tokenization and our core business going forward. We continue to work collaboratively with the issuers and network partners and other infrastructure partners, as Tom mentioned. Post closing, we'll have more to say about our go-to-market efforts. But that guidance today does reflect essentially the environment we're in today where prices are down and there are other macro headwinds that we think will slow the rate of growth into the early part of next year. We need to incorporate that into our outlook. Again, everyone knows we're in the middle of a pretty deep crypto bear market here.

And so for the sake of providing an outlook that reflects where we are today, we thought it was most appropriate to layer in some of those headwinds, which are also -- as I discussed, is impacting the change in the SS&O range to remove the high end and narrow the range towards the lower end.

Operator: And our next question will come from Dan Welden from Wells Fargo.

Daniel F. Welden: Tom, I wanted to ask you, Equiniti seems levered to the number of listed companies overall. And there's been a lot of initiatives in the U.S. over time to try to make it easier and less friction to publicly list. And I wonder, in your new role in the markets post Equiniti, how you think about the prospects of more listings, reducing friction points, rule changes and how you can play a role in that?

Thomas Farley: Yes. I think that's a really thoughtful question. When we were contemplating the Equiniti transaction back in the first 2 quarters of the year, that was definitely one of the vectors we were thinking about: just total addressable market size and the total addressable market size growth over time.

The other was just the absolute size of the pie for the transfer agent function in a world where shares are moving on-chain and the transfer agent offering is getting less commoditized, more highly specialized, more value-add, offers new services that transfer agents haven't typically provided, such as what I described to Owen: the provision of the smart contracts, the provision of the whitelist, the connectivity to various new types of venues, liquidity provision, so on and so forth, all the sorts of things that Bullish was kind of perfectly enabled to provide.

And I have to be candid, we put a whole lot more faith in the latter than the former, meaning we put a whole lot more faith in the growing of the TAM because of the increasingly strategic role of the transfer agent. I remember when we announced the deal, there was some sort of eyebrow raising like, "Oh, wow, this transfer agent function, how important is it?" Well, fast-forward, others have woken up to, "Wow, this is a very critical role," from the Chairman of the SEC to many analysts who cover our business. Certainly, that feels right. But in terms of will the number of public companies grow, I'm gun-shy.

As the head of the New York Stock Exchange back in the day, I convinced myself that things were changing. We were in a deregulatory environment, we were going to see a lot more public companies, things like the JOBS Act would result in many more companies going public. It simply hasn't happened. I do have a small hope, but I don't want to oversell you on it, that actually blockchain technology itself is going to allow for far more efficient capital raising, broader capital raising and an easier go-to-market path for companies, and that ultimately will result in more public companies. But we're not banking on it.

We didn't bank on it when we made the decision to acquire Equiniti. And we're looking at other things like can we grow the TAM by providing more of these value-added services and can we grow our business geographically.

Operator: And our next question will come from Gareth Gacetta from Cantor.

Gareth Gacetta: I just kind of wanted to double-click on the updated medium-term outlook. I know the SEC's innovation exemption has some caps on kind of the growth of regulated tokenization in the U.S. So, I'm wondering if you could talk about kind of what the realistic ceiling is on tokenization revenue over the near term here? And what maybe has to happen for that ceiling to lift or for the restrictions to kind of be lower going forward?

Thomas Farley: Yes. No, I appreciate it. Let me go full [ nerd alert ] on you, but do it really quickly. The innovation exemption -- the word exemption, I'll come back to that, but focus on that. What the innovation exemption did is it said, if you operate a platform in the following broad way, you are exempt from registering for regulation with the SEC and you can operate your platform and you can trade third-party tokens, and it's really kind of oriented towards those third-party tokens or issuer tokens, but a little bit less oriented towards those issuer tokens. Why did I answer your question by starting in that capacity? That's one small subset of on-chain trading.

Where we expect the bulk of on-chain trading to come from in the United States is from regulated venues, which are ATSs, automated trading systems affiliated with broker-dealers or national securities exchanges. The caps that you referred to, to be clear, only refer to trading that occurs on these so-called TSVs, these exempt venues. I applaud the SEC for pushing forward with the innovation exemption to get kind of the party started, if you will.

But ultimately -- and you've seen this with the announcements from the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq -- ultimately, I expect from players like the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq and others, Bullish, that you will see far more trading ultimately on regulated venues in the United States of on-chain shares than on TSVs. I hope that answered your question.

Operator: Our next question will come from Michael Kim from Bloomberg.

Michael Kim: Based on month-to-date data, it looks like your trading volumes have picked up thus far in November. So, just curious if you might have seen any material shifts in market shares just following the events at Binance? And then just given your focus on compliance and licensing, is there an opportunity to maybe capitalize on a renewed focus on security really across the industry?

David Bonanno: Appreciate the question. With regard to the monthly trading metrics, as we've mentioned in the past, our trading activity and therefore, our market share, particularly in spot markets, is most heavily driven by volatility. So, the higher the volatility, the better we tend to perform with our institutional customer base on a volume market share basis. With regard to the events at Binance, I can't say today that we really see direct impact that's attributable to that event. That said, we do think it's another reminder to market participants that they take risks when they're on unregulated venues.

And we do think that over time, market share will continue to inure to mature regulated venues that operate themselves to the highest standards of professionalism, security, safety and compliance. And so we think the trend remains in our favor. And then again, on the monthly trading metrics, mostly driven by volatility. Again, we tend to outperform in highly volatile environments given our customer base.

Operator: And our next question will come from Will Johnston from Canaccord Genuity.

William Johnston: Maybe just one on tokenized shares. I think Bullish tokenized shares have been trading on the platform for a few months now. So, just any learnings or early learnings from that and how holders are using them in unique ways and maybe any way this has shaped conversations or things you're putting in front of other issuers?

Thomas Farley: Sure. Oh boy, I'm going to go high level for a second. I think looking into the crystal ball is a little bit fuzzy of exactly how all of this is going to develop. What isn't fuzzy for us is that shares in the global securities market, which incidentally is $275 trillion, is going to move on to public blockchains for settlement, for registry and then certainly for transferring, moving around, pledging shares as collateral because that is where the most efficiency is going to come from. There's analyst reports that as much as $1 trillion will be pulled out of the system that today is just tied up and really is not tied up in a fruitful way.

With respect to trading, 1 could imagine sort of a single monolithic trading or liquidity environment that's independent of how that share is being traded. What do I mean by that? Today, when you trade on Nasdaq, you don't know if the person you're trading with is settling in a paper share or an electronic share. Tomorrow, you might be unaware are they trading in a paper share, an electronic share or an on-chain share. And then the on-chain share market share will just simply grow from 0 to something approaching 100%. And the industrial logic to me would point in that direction.

However, in the meantime, there's a whole bunch of people out there building platforms to demonstrate how good this public blockchain is. And so it requires some liquidity for the tokenized shares, in particular, for the on-chain shares in particular. And so that's what's kind of forming up, and that was kind of the gist of your question. And I want to tell you, it's not dead easy, and this is part of what Dave and I have been talking about on this call about how quick the adoption will be for tokenized trading. It's not dead easy to predict because there are some challenges to creating that initial liquidity.

And one of those challenges is simply the ability to quickly move from a paper share or electronic share to a tokenized share and then back into a paper share or an electronic share. And we have some things in the works that we look forward to sharing more with you about in the days and weeks ahead that will facilitate that and will kind of grease the skids and it will give us a clear pathway and I think will be very, very helpful to our issuers and to the market at large. But we're not quite yet ready to declare victory and share all those details, but stay tuned.

Operator: I am showing no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the call back over to Tom Farley for any closing remarks.

Thomas Farley: I just want to say thank you all for listening. Thank you all for bearing with us. As Dave and I said, it's been a tough crypto environment with prices down by half and unfortunately, not getting the Clarity Act. We've never been as excited as we are. It's perhaps a bit counterintuitive. We think we're really well positioned. We thought that in May, but we were a little nervous with the announcement of Equiniti. It's a certainty now in our minds that the market is moving in our direction, and we are going to be able to be very, very helpful to issuers in many different ways.

And we feel good about this strategic portfolio of products and services that we pulled together over the last half decade or more and coupling it with Equiniti, we think, is going to give us a chance to really delight issuers and put some money in shareholders' pockets. So, thank you very much. Thanks also to Dave and to Liam and our team for their preparation for this earnings call.

Operator: This concludes today's conference. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3133. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

Which new iPhone Duo features in iOS 27.3 are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.

#3132. The CEO behind GTA VI doesn’t play games. Analysts say he bet up to $1.5B

Strauss Zelnick says being a gamer doesn't make a better boss, and his biggest bet launches on Thursday.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has run the company since 2011.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick does not play the games his company sells, Fortune reported, as GTA VI launches with an estimated $1B to $1.5B budget. Take-Two has not confirmed the cost, but the game has tied Metacritic’s record score and pre-orders beat expectations.

Strauss Zelnick has run Take-Two Interactive, which owns GTA studio Rockstar, since 2011. He does not play the games it sells, Fortune reported in a profile republished on Wednesday, the eve of Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch.

“I don’t think being consumer-in-chief really helps a CEO be effective in this business,” Zelnick told Business Insider.

Analysts cited by Business Insider estimate GTA VI cost $1B to $1.5B to make. Take-Two has not confirmed a figure, and Zelnick has only said the game “was expensive”.

The bet looks set to pay off. GTA VI tied Metacritic’s all-time record with a score of 99, and Take-Two said pre-orders beat expectations. Sensor Tower data puts pre-orders at 17 million, according to Fortune.

The game costs from $80 and comes without a physical disc, as Sony plans to stop making discs for new games from 2028. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold more than 215 million copies since 2013.

Under Zelnick, Take-Two’s shares have risen more than 1,700%, and its revenue grew roughly fivefold to $5.6B in 2025. He has also said generative AI played no part in making GTA VI, which Rockstar built by hand.

#3129. J&J Snacks (JJSF) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins expanded as frozen beverage growth offset a food service slowdown.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 3:55PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

J&J Snack Foods (JJSF +9.53%) management reported a stabilization in the sales environment during the final period of the fiscal year, noting that the strategic transition away from specific bakery product lines is now complete. The company is transitioning into the next phase of its operational efficiency program, which focuses on manufacturing uptime and network optimization to counter ongoing logistics headwinds. Strategic priorities for the upcoming fiscal year include scaling recent product innovations in retail channels and expanding beverage distribution into international convenience markets. Management indicated a focus on balancing promotional investments with volume growth to support continued margin expansion.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the J&J Snack Foods Fourth Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Reed Anderson with ICR. Sir, please go ahead.

Reed Anderson: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining the J&J Snack Foods Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter Conference Call. Before getting started, let me take a minute to read the safe harbor language. This call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. All statements made on this call that do not relate to matters of historical facts shall be considered forward-looking statements, including statements regarding management's plans, strategies, goals, expectations and objectives as well as our anticipated financial performance. This includes, without limitation, our expectations with respect to the success of our cost savings initiatives and customer demand improvements in the sales channels in which we operate.

These statements are neither promises nor guarantees and involve known and unknown risks, uncertainties and other important factors that may cause results, performance or achievements to be materially different from any future results, performance or achievements expressed or implied by the forward-looking statements. Risk factors and other items discussed in our annual report on Form 10-K and our other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission could cause actual results to differ materially from those indicated by the forward-looking statements made on the call today. Any such forward-looking statements represent management's estimates as of the date of this call today, November 18, 2026.

While we may elect to update forward-looking statements at some point in the future, we disclaim any obligation to do so even if subsequent events cause expectations to change. In addition, we may also reference certain non-GAAP measures on the call today, including adjusted EBITDA, adjusted operating income or adjusted earnings per share, all of which are reconciled to the nearest GAAP measure on the company's earnings press release, which can be found in the Investor Relations section of our website. Joining me on the call today is Dan Fachner, our Chief Executive Officer; along with Shawn Munsell, our Chief Financial Officer. Following management's prepared remarks, we will open the call for a question-and-answer session.

With that, I would like to turn the call over to Mr. Fachner. Please go ahead, Dan.

Daniel Fachner: Good morning, and thanks, everyone, for joining today's call to discuss our fourth quarter results. As we signaled on the last call, the sales environment improved in the fourth quarter, and our transformation initiatives continued to support our performance. Gross profit increased $6.6 million to $136.9 million, and gross margin expanded 200 basis points to 33.7%. Adjusted EBITDA came in at $53.3 million compared to $57.4 million last year, and adjusted earnings per share were $1.39 versus $1.58 a year ago. Distribution costs were the primary headwind to earnings in the quarter, up 21.6% or $9.1 million due to significantly higher freight and fuel costs. Net sales were $406 million, down 1%.

We were pleased to see the SUPERPRETZEL brand front and center nationwide, and we received great consumer feedback. In retail, net sales increased 17.1%, driven by promotional activity and seasonal churro sales. Syndicated data for the 13 weeks ending October 4 continued to show good momentum across many of our retail brands. Dogsters retail sales were up 28% in tracked channels. Retail Dippin' Dots sales were up more than 90% and Luigi's was up about 9%, while SUPERPRETZEL was up 3%. The high-temp Dippin' Dots product is now in about 7,300 stores. In Frozen Beverage, beverage dollar sales rose 18.6%, more than offsetting the decline in machine and service sales.

Beverage strength was led by theaters and supported by amusement, convenience and other channels. We continue to expect to close the service revenue gap in fiscal '27. Distribution costs remain our biggest challenge. We have taken action to mitigate some of the pressure by maximizing load sizes and reducing distance of haul wherever we can. We have more initiatives underway for fiscal '27. However, we still expect distribution cost pressure to persist for the foreseeable future. Briefly looking at full year results. Adjusted EBITDA was $176.4 million, down approximately 2.4% from $180.9 million last year. Net sales declined 4% with the anticipated reduction in bakery sales representing an approximate 3% headwind for the year.

We made significant progress on our strategic plan for fiscal '26. Notably, we achieved our targeted run rate of $25 million of annualized savings under Project Apollo. Our gross margin expanded by 210 basis points to 31.8% for the year, enabled by Project Apollo as well as favorable mix improvements as we focus on our core products. We successfully launched several new products as part of our strategic plan, including retail Dippin' Dots, Dogsters Sandwiches, Protein Pretzels and Luigi's Mini Pops with better-for-you attributes. We expect these sales to continue to build in the coming year. We continue to see growth in Food Service pretzel sales for the fiscal year, up about 5%.

The beverage component of our Frozen Beverage business rose 9.7%, underpinned by higher theater traffic as well as other channel growth. We remain focused on growing gallon volumes. Retail sales grew 4% as we increased promotions to support volume, innovation and to protect shelf space. Although top line growth was successful, we plan to modify our promotional activity in '27 to better balance volume and financial performance. We bought back $74 million in stock and finished the year with no debt and more than $90 million of cash on the balance sheet. Now looking ahead, we are entering fiscal '27 with some real momentum.

Regarding the top line, we are expecting to return to growth in fiscal '27 through a combination of core volume growth, innovation, mix improvements and pricing. Growth will include several product launches such as new high-temp Dippin' Dots flavors for retail, Dr Pepper and ICEE, new Luigi's tubes at retail, SUPERPRETZEL buns for retail and Food Service, which leveraged the success of the recent promotion with a major QSR and SUPERPRETZEL branded Bavarian pull-aparts for Food Service, a product that I'm really excited about in '27. Frozen Beverage has an encouraging setup for the coming year. Although we had strong movie performances in the back half of fiscal '26, the outlook for '27 is quite promising.

The lineup includes new movies from the Jumanji, Spider-Man, Sonic and Shrek franchises. The box office that aligns to our fiscal year is projected to increase about 3% versus '26. We are making progress on our plan to close the service revenue gap and expect to be there by the second quarter. We are seeing encouraging activity with new and existing partners across theaters, convenience and entertainment venues. The team continues to be focused on growing gallon volumes through promotional activity and new account tests in place. The West Coast QSR test continues, but the time line has been longer than anticipated.

However, we are pleased to share that we are launching new business with a major convenience chain in Mexico with the rollout to be completed in the second half of fiscal '27. We are implementing new Apollo initiatives that will drive approximately $5 million of incremental annualized benefits, building on the $25 million we implemented in fiscal '26. We are targeting $3 million in manufacturing savings and $2 million in distribution savings. We expect to be materially complete during the fiscal third quarter. Ingredient costs are expected to be moderately inflationary in fiscal '27 with pressure from packaging, shortening, oils and flour more than offsetting lower chocolate costs.

Finally, we continue to evaluate options for some of the noncore components of our portfolio and we will continue to drive margin improvements as seen this past year. I'll now hand things over to Shawn, who will walk you through the numbers in more detail. Shawn?

Growth was primarily driven by frozen novelties and retail churros. Retail segment operating income decreased $3.9 million, driven primarily by higher promotional investment, higher distribution costs and favorable insurance recoveries in the prior year. Frozen Beverage segment net sales increased $6.1 million or 6.1% to $105.7 million. Beverage sales increased 18.6%, but were partially offset by lower machine and service sales. Frozen Beverage segment operating income increased $2.7 million to $21.4 million as higher gross profit outweighed distribution cost pressure. Consolidated gross margin improved 200 basis points to 33.7%, supported by plant consolidation savings, mix improvements, raw material cost improvements, partly offset by higher promotional investment in retail.

Total operating expenses were $92 million or 22.7% of sales compared to 29% in the prior year quarter. Operating expenses in the quarter included a net nonrecurring gain of approximately $11.9 million, largely driven by a $16 million gain from insurance proceeds. Prior year quarter operating expenses included nonrecurring operating expenses of approximately $24.8 million, driven primarily by plant closure expenses. Selling and marketing expenses increased approximately 1.6% or $500,000 to $33.1 million, representing about 8.2% of sales compared to 7.9% in the prior year. Distribution expenses increased 21.6% or $9.1 million to $51.3 million and accounted for 12.6% of sales compared to 10.3% in the prior year period, driven by higher freight and fuel costs.

We expect distribution costs to remain elevated in fiscal 2027. Administrative expenses increased 15.3% to $22 million or 5.4% of sales and included $2.7 million of nonrecurring legal expenses. Excluding nonrecurring items, administrative expenses increased about 1.3%. Adjusted operating income was $34.5 million compared to $37.7 million in the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA was $53.3 million, down 7.1% from $57.4 million last year. The effective tax rate for the quarter was approximately 25.7% as compared to 4.8% in the prior year quarter. The lower effective tax rate in the prior year quarter primarily reflected a change in estimate on our blended state tax rate and the corresponding impact on the valuation of our net deferred tax liabilities.

On a reported basis, earnings per diluted share were $1.80 compared to $0.58 per share last year, with the current quarter benefiting from a nonrecurring insurance gain, and the prior year affected by nonrecurring plant closure expenses. On an adjusted basis, earnings per share were $1.39 compared to $1.58 a year ago. Our balance sheet remains strong with $90.3 million of cash and no debt at quarter end. During the quarter, we generated approximately $69.7 million in operating cash flow and invested $17.6 million in capital expenditures. For the full year, we generated $170.2 million of operating cash flow and invested $70.9 million in capital expenditures. We repurchased $74 million in stock during fiscal 2026.

That concludes our prepared remarks, and we're now ready to take your questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is going to come from the line of Todd Brooks with Benchmark StoneX.

Todd Brooks: Congrats on the results in the quarter and getting off on the right foot here going into the new fiscal year. So good to see.

Todd Brooks: A couple of questions, if I may. And Shawn, I think this would probably be helpful for everybody. Can you frame up the thoughts on distribution costs and how we should be thinking about it in '27? I know the situation is fluid. I know there's a diesel component, but there's also just kind of the cost of lanes and routes now because of some driver pressure that may not go away. Can you maybe walk us through if you can put it in a percent of sales basis or something along those lines for how much incremental pressure you would expect on the distribution line? And you hinted at maybe steps to mitigate some of that.

Can you review the work that's being done there as well?

Daniel Fachner: Todd, this is Dan. That's a great question and one we really need to focus in on. And I'm going to turn this back over to Shawn to do that in just a moment. But I kind of wanted to start off with just a few comments. Fiscal '26, we thought was a really strong year for J&J Snack Foods and with the trends improving in the fourth quarter even. We set out to expand margins and reduce expenses and refocus on the business on the core and the team really delivered. I'm proud of what the team accomplished and really optimistic about '27. We're encouraged by the momentum and expect top line growth this coming year.

The planned bakery is now behind us, and that removes that headwind. Our new product initiatives are performing well. We're coming to market with some new products in addition to that. We see new business opportunities across the portfolio. And at the same time, as you just talked about, we're realistic about some of the challenges ahead, really particularly those distribution costs. However, we expect that to remain elevated through the year, but our network initiatives should help offset some of those costs. And then with pricing and volume growth, which we see is real, we believe that we can still expand our margins.

So with that, I'm going to let Shawn dig into some of the details that you just asked about and talk about those distribution costs.

Shawn Munsell: Yes. So obviously, we're up 21.6% distribution costs in the quarter. Most of that was really driven by freight and fuel. And it's really the freight cost that's having the biggest impact on the P&L. As it stands today, we have seen some declines in diesel prices this quarter. We hit a record or near record here in -- unfortunately, in the quarter of over $6. I see the EIA is reporting that's just below $6 a gallon now. So we do expect to see some fuel relief. As it relates to freight, at least for the foreseeable future, it does feel like it's going to remain elevated. We are taking some steps to mitigate that pressure.

Essentially, the teams have been working on reconfiguring our pallet sizes to ensure that we're packing as much as we can on a truck and reducing the number of trucks that we have to utilize to get our products to market. We've even moved a small quantity of product to rail transportation to take advantage of some savings. And there are some instances where we've been able to shift production from within our manufacturing network just to get closer to the customer. So for now, it feels like it's going to remain elevated.

And I think that once we get to the second half, once we get to about May or June of next year, we'll start to lap the increase that will really kick in over the summer.

Daniel Fachner: Team's really heavily focused on that, Todd, and we'll continue to monitor and watch it closely and pull every lever that we can.

Todd Brooks: That's great. And just so, Shawn, the shape of it, maybe expect the year-over-year pressure in the first half and then we get back to a neutral to maybe slightly favorable place in the second half of the year then?

Shawn Munsell: Yes, that's right. We do see a chance for there to be some favorability in the second half.

Todd Brooks: Okay. Great. And then, Dan, I wanted to follow up with you because you have pointed to being able to drive organic revenue growth in fiscal '27 and another strong roster of innovation that you laid out earlier. You made a comment on the call, though, that there could be more evaluation of noncore portfolio items. So I want to understand within that guidance for organic growth in the business, we're through the bakery rationalization or that's my understanding. What else are you looking at in the portfolio? And would the organic growth actually be some element of basis points stronger, but you are expecting to rationalize some of the other business lines in '27?

Daniel Fachner: Yes. I don't expect there to be any further rationalization, Todd, in our business. We're going to continue to evaluate the areas of our business that aren't core. We're seeing some really great growth within our core business today, and you even saw that over this last quarter with some great growth in churros and pretzels. But we're going to continue to evaluate opportunities and possibilities for some of those products that don't sit within our core. But that will not include SKU rationalization in 2027.

Operator: Our next question is going to come from the line of David Shakno with William Blair.

David Shakno: David Shakno on for Jon Andersen. Congrats on the nice quarter. So gross margin was solidly above last year. I think you said 200 basis points ahead of consensus, too. Could you give us a sense, even ballpark how much of that came from Apollo versus mix and raw material deflation? And then you mentioned in the prepared remarks, I think you said you expect raw material inflation for fiscal '27. I wanted to get a sense if that's more back half weighted given the tailwinds this past quarter? Or do you expect kind of that inflationary pressure right away and to persist throughout the year? And then one follow-up after that.

Daniel Fachner: Great. David, good to talk to you. Thank you for being on today. Tell Jon, we missed him. Thanks for pointing out that gross margin. We talked a lot about over the last few years about growing the margin and getting it back into that 30s range and then with goals to get even above that at some point. So really proud of what the team accomplished this year by driving the gross margin and expect that we can continue to do that this next year. It did raise about 210 basis points for the year. I think we ended the year somewhere around 31.8% and proud of being able to do that.

Hopefully, next year, we can get ourselves into that 32% range or above. We do have some inflationary issues, and I'm going to let Shawn discuss those with you as we get into '27.

Shawn Munsell: Yes, that's right. So if you think about the Apollo impact, that was just -- it was about almost $20 million in the fiscal year, that we achieved behind the Apollo initiatives. Remember, we were about $3.5 million in the first quarter, and then we got up over $4 million in savings from the plant consolidation. And then we hit the full run rate there in the second half. So close to $20 million worth of impact that's going to be sustainable in those earnings.

As far as the inflation is concerned, we do see that more of a back half probably kicking in a little bit more in the second and the third quarter, but we don't see the intensity of that inflation kicking in, in Q1.

David Shakno: Got it. That makes sense. And then one other thing here. Can you help us understand what list price increases you've taken or announced for fiscal '27? I know historically, ICEE pricing comes beginning of the calendar year, I believe. But I wanted to understand where else more broadly, if it's ICEE and other things too, more broadly, which segments? Are they in market yet, kind of plans for the upcoming year across the portfolio there?

Daniel Fachner: Yes. Great. Thank you, David. We do have plans for a price increase this year. Those will take in effect in January. With the ICEE and the Dippin' Dots, we're probably somewhere in that 3% range. Snack food side will be a little bit more surgical, but will be -- by the time that we get that included with ICEE and Dippin' Dots, probably an overall increase of around the 2.5% range, something in that neighborhood.

David Shakno: 2.5% for the total company?

Daniel Fachner: For the total. Yes, total overall.

Operator: Our next question will be from the line of Scott Marks with Jefferies.

Scott Marks: Just wanted to follow up on the conversation you just had just about the pricing impact as we think about that for fiscal '27. What are you anticipating on the volume side now that you're through the SKU rationalizations, you have these innovations coming to market. Curious if you're baking in any elasticity impacts or just overall, how we should be thinking about that dynamic?

Daniel Fachner: Yes. We think we'll have positive volume impact in the year. We like some of the great things that we're doing with our core products. We mentioned that already, and they'll continue to grow. What I really like is our innovation this past year and some more innovation coming the following year. And one of the things that Lynwood Mallard always reminds us of on innovation is it kind of grows over a 2-, 3-year period. And so we think that, that will be a positive impact on our growth this coming year. Somewhere in the neighborhood I think innovation will add somewhere in the neighborhood of 1%.

So when you kind of think about the pricing and the innovation and getting our service revenue back to even, and we think that will happen in the second quarter. We think we'll be somewhere in that low to mid-single-digit growth rate for next year.

Daniel Fachner: Yes. Well, the great thing about the Food Service is that's the area where we had that heavy SKU rationalization, and that's coming to end. So we feel good about that. We have some really good growth going on in our core products with more pretzel growth and churro growth. Both of those, we had a big QSR that ran a pretzel bun promotion with us that had SUPERPRETZEL front and center, which was great. We've got a new piece of business with churros back in a retail club store that's doing really well for us. I think Food Service is on its way to having a decent year. And the real key is getting the rationalization behind us.

Scott Marks: Okay. And maybe if I could just squeeze in one more. Project Apollo, you talked about kind of Phase 2 kicking in. And I know there's been discussions about like what happens beyond Apollo? How do you continue to improve the automation and the network and the efficiency. Wondering if you can just tell us maybe a little bit longer term, how you're thinking about kind of even the next phase beyond what's in place for this year?

Shawn Munsell: Yes. So this next phase that we've just launched, the incremental $5 million, $3 million coming from manufacturing efficiencies and $2 million coming from further distribution optimization. As it relates to what's happening in the plants, the team has a number of projects that are going to drive that $3 million. It's a handful of items that are really going to be driving a reduction in waste, higher uptime, and we feel pretty good about it. We're also going to be rolling out this year where -- it's actually underway now, the rollout is, what I'd call some plant floor systems that will help us in that cause. We're rolling out Redzone.

I think that most folks are familiar with that system. We're also making some improvements to our warehouse management tools, and that's going to help to drive some of those savings.

Daniel Fachner: Both of those initiatives will help really drive plant efficiency projects inside the plant. Redzone gives us real-time information on the line where people have handhelds and are able to see it and then post it around the building. We're pretty excited about it. It's a program that's used a lot in the industry in manufacturing and something that I think will be very helpful for us this coming year.

Operator: Thank you. And I'm showing no further questions. And I would like to hand the conference back over to Dan Fachner for closing remarks.

Daniel Fachner: Great. Thank you, operator. Thanks, everyone, for your questions. Stepping back, I think the fourth quarter results show that the strategic plan is working. The team at J&J is embracing the plan and executing with excellence. Gross margin expanded again, the sales environment improved across our core products, and we are managing through distribution cost pressures. We enter fiscal '27 with a stronger core portfolio, a more efficient cost structure and a strong balance sheet, and we expect to return to top line growth. So thank you again for your support, and we look forward to catching up again next quarter. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude today's program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a great day.

#3127. Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share, valuing it at about $1.5tn

The Anthropic IPO is set to raise at least $68bn, plus a $26bn placement, beating SpaceX. Shares in the Claude maker start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday as ANT.

Dario Amodei speaks at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos, 20 January 2026

Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it marketed, people familiar with the matter told Natasha Mascarenhas and Bailey Lipschultz of Bloomberg, who reported the price first. The company also sold more shares than it planned. Its stock starts trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

At $83, Anthropic is worth about $1.49tn on a fully diluted basis, the Financial Times reported. Other outlets have since confirmed the price with their own sources. Anthropic has not announced it.

The company had been weighing a price well above $80, and orders had reached close to seven times the shares on offer by Sunday.

Anthropic had marketed 801.4 million shares, and its seven co-founders offered another 23.6 million, Bloomberg reported. With the higher price, the Anthropic IPO should raise at least $68bn. A $26bn private placement with strategic partners, at the same price, takes the total past $94bn.

That beats SpaceX, which raised $75bn in its June IPO, or $86.2bn once its bankers sold extra shares. Anthropic’s bankers have the same option, the FT reported, so the total could still rise.

By value, it would be the second-biggest IPO ever, behind SpaceX’s $1.77tn debut, Fortune reported.

Buyers should try “not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms”, Anthropic wrote in its prospectus, the FT reported.

The company said profits would be balanced against “the public good”.

Investors expected a $2tn valuation over the summer, the FT reported. The IPO lands as AI stocks slide. The Nasdaq 100 has lost 13% since its early October peak, according to the FT. Nvidia fell for a fifth day on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported, a week after Jensen Huang’s exit as chief executive.

The offering will leave Anthropic with more than $200bn on its balance sheet, the FT reported. The company plans to spend that on compute and infrastructure. According to its investors, it would rather not sell shares again, and it wants an investment-grade credit rating so it can borrow instead.

It already carries $6.2bn of debt, which it calls “substantial” in its filings, the Associated Press reported. Its long-term benefit trust will be able to elect or remove a majority of the board.

The listing is also a payday for Anthropic’s venture backers, several of which planned to buy more shares in the offering.

#3125. iOS 27.3 adds Siri AI usage limits, here’s what counts toward your limit

Earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn

In a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

One question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The company shares just two examples of something advanced:

really disappointing to see Apple embedding the AI scam into their devices and services. Siri has been so easy to disable and ignore for the last 15 years but in the last few years as Apple has bought more and more into the AI scam they're shoving it deeper into their ecosystem and making it more and more of a hassle to disable and ignore

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”

It would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for users. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

What do you think of Siri AI’s parameters for advanced requests in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.
